title: The usefulness of YouTube videos on lung cancer
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on lung cancer. Two independent physicians classified each video as useful (scientifically correct), misleading (containing at least one scientifically unproven statement) or neither, and the paper reports the share of items classified misleading with an explicit denominator (8 of 143, 5.6%). This is an explicit misleading/veracity coding against expert judgement, so it meets the CONTENT criterion.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube videos, no country restriction; study run in Denmark)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on lung cancer classified as misleading
estimates.value_raw: 8 (5.6%) videos were considered misleading (Table 3, Total: Misleading 8 (5.6); Abstract rounds this to '8 (6%)')
estimates.denominator: 143 eligible videos of the 167 most-viewed 'lung cancer' YouTube videos (all videos down to 30,000 views), after excluding 18 non-English and 6 unrelated videos
estimates.definition: A video was coded 'misleading' if it contained at least one scientifically unproven piece of information on the study's content categories; 'useful' if it contained scientifically correct information; 'neither' if it was not misleading but gave no useful medical information
estimates.misinfo_def: 'misleading' (containing at least one scientifically unproven information)
estimates.source_quote: 8 (5.6%) videos were considered misleading. All 8 videos
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. e341; Table 3 (Usefulness category by source, Total row)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent physicians (HM and HM) rated each video's usefulness; Cohen's Kappa for inter-rater agreement on the classification of the videos = 0.82 ('almost perfect agreement'). No validated instrument was used; the authors state no validated tool exists for YouTube video assessment.
estimates.moderator_quote: A search of YouTube (http://www.youtube.com) was performed between the 12 July 2021 and 6 August 2021, using the search term ‘lung cancer.’ ... The filter ‘sorted by views’ was applied and all videos down to 30 000 views were initially reviewed. ... The usefulness of the information provided was assessed by two independent physicians (HM and HM), using three categories including ‘useful’ (containing scientifically correct information on any of the above-mentioned categories) and ‘misleading’ (containing at least one scientifically unproven information).
estimates.notes: The source_quote stops at the two-column break in the PDF; the full passage reads '8 (5.6%) videos were considered misleading. All 8 videos were related to alternative remedies for cancer prevention or treatment. 6 out of the 8 videos with misleading content were videos on risk factors, including “cancer fighting foods” and how consumption of these specific foods can prevent or lower the risk of getting cancer.' The corpus is a rank-truncated, most-viewed set (30,000-view floor) for a single health topic, hence denom_scope topical with denom_selection curated. The 'misleading' label is veracity-based (scientifically unproven or incorrect content, all 8 concerned alternative remedies), so the row is CONTENT rather than QUALITY, though the wording 'at least one scientifically unproven information' is broader than strictly false, which is why breadth is coded misleading. Abstract gives 6% (rounded); the Results and Table 3 give 5.6%, which is the value kept.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the 62% (89/143) classified 'useful' and the 32% (46/143) 'neither' — complements of the misleading share, not misinformation prevalence in their own right; (2) the misleading share broken down by uploader source in Table 3 (non-medical provider 4/33 = 12.1%; associations 1/23 = 4.3%; university/governmental/hospitals 2/45 = 4.4%; TV/news/YouTube channel 1/36 = 2.8%; physicians and academic sources 0%) — these are subgroup rows, not the paper's headline, so per the rules only the main figure is kept; (3) engagement comparisons (median views 845,643 for misleading vs 81,700 for useful, etc.) — not shares. No DISCERN/JAMA/GQS instrument was used in this paper.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. YouTube searched 12 July - 6 August 2021 for 'lung cancer' without login and in Incognito mode; 12,500 results, sorted by views, all videos down to 30,000 views reviewed, giving 167 videos, of which 143 eligible (18 non-English and 6 unrelated excluded). Two independent physicians classified each video useful/misleading/neither; Cohen's Kappa 0.82. Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests in SPSS 28.0. No validated instrument; authors note the absence of one as a limitation, and note the 30,000-view cut-off means the corpus is not the whole platform.
rob.item6_quote: The usefulness of the information provided was assessed by two independent physicians (HM and HM), using three categories including ‘useful’ (containing scientifically correct information on any of the above-mentioned categories) and ‘misleading’ (containing at least one scientifically unproven information).
rob.item10_quote: 89 videos (62%) were classified as useful, 8 (6%) as misleading and 46 (32%) as neither.
